title: Philosophy: Big Ideas · Episode 2
chapters: Ubuntu: I am because we are
Philosophy's golden age in the Islamic world
Three ways to decide what's right

units.t: Philosophy: Big Ideas. Episode two.
In this episode: Ubuntu: I am because we are, Philosophy's golden age in the Islamic world, Machiavelli: the man behind ‘The Prince’ and Three ways to decide what's right.
Part one. Ubuntu: I am because we are.
A person is a person through other people.
This idea from southern Africa helped guide a nation through its transition from apartheid, and it offers a challenge to the way many Western philosophies picture the self.
I see you.
In many parts of southern Africa, a common greeting translates roughly as 'I see you', and the reply as 'I am here'.
The exchange hints at a philosophy in which existence is affirmed through recognition by others.
It is often summed up in the word ubuntu, found in Nguni languages such as isiZulu and isiXhosa, with related words across many Bantu languages.
Ubuntu is usually translated as 'humanness' or 'humanity towards others', and captured in the isiZulu saying umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu: 'a person is a person through other persons'.
It is not one written theory by a founding philosopher.
It is a living ethical outlook, carried in proverbs, customs and everyday expectations, which thinkers have more recently set out systematically.
The relational self.
Many influential Western philosophies start with the individual.
Descartes began with a single mind doubting everything; social contract theorists imagined separate individuals agreeing to form a society.
Ubuntu starts elsewhere, treating people as fundamentally bound up with one another.
On many accounts, personhood is not just a biological fact but something you grow into by how you treat others.
In everyday speech in some communities, a person who behaves cruelly or selfishly may be said to lack ubuntu, or even to be 'not a person', meaning not living up to what a human should be.
The Kenyan-born philosopher John Mbiti put a related African communal outlook in 1969: 'I am, because we are; and since we are, therefore I am.'
What it asks of you.
In practice, ubuntu is associated with sharing with those in need, welcoming strangers, respecting elders, and repairing damaged relationships rather than simply punishing.
A frequently told illustration is a traveller passing through a village, who would expect to be offered food and water without having to ask.
The American-born philosopher Thaddeus Metz, who works in South Africa, has tried to state its core precisely.
On an ubuntu view, he suggests, right actions respect and promote harmonious relationships, where people identify with one another and act for each other's good.
Wrong actions are unfriendly or divisive.
That makes ubuntu different from both rule-based and outcome-based ethics: the focus is the quality of relationships.
Reconciliation and law.
Ubuntu became internationally known during South Africa's transition to democracy.
The 1993 interim Constitution said there was 'a need for ubuntu but not for victimisation'.
Archbishop Desmond Tutu, who chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, explained his approach through ubuntu.
The commission offered amnesty to some perpetrators who fully disclosed politically motivated crimes, and gave victims a public platform.
Tutu argued that dehumanising others diminishes the oppressor too, and that healing requires restoring relationships.
Some victims felt justice was sacrificed.
In 1995, in S v Makwanyane, the Constitutional Court ruled the death penalty unconstitutional.
Several judges cited ubuntu as valuing life and dignity and favouring reconciliation over retribution.
Critics say the concept is too broad to guide judges clearly.
Debates and wider voices.
Ubuntu has thoughtful critics, including African philosophers.
Some say it has become a slogan, used in corporate training until it means little more than 'teamwork'.
Others warn against romanticising a single 'African' worldview across hundreds of cultures.
A deeper worry concerns rights: if personhood depends on community, what protects dissenters or people marginalised by their own communities?
Defenders reply that ubuntu condemns treating anyone as less than human.
Kwame Gyekye proposed a 'moderate communitarianism' giving both community and individual rights their due.
Other African philosophers include Kwasi Wiredu, who urged 'conceptual decolonisation', and Henry Odera Oruka, who recorded the reasoning of local sages.
Ubuntu leaves a question worth asking: how much of who you are was made by other people?
The key idea: Ubuntu is a southern African idea that we become fully human through our relationships with others.
Part two. Philosophy's golden age in the Islamic world.
Between Ancient Greece and the European Renaissance, some of the boldest philosophy on Earth was written in Arabic.
Meet the thinkers who preserved Aristotle, argued about cause and effect, and imagined a man floating in the air.
Reason meets revelation.
From the late 700s, Greek philosophy was translated into Arabic under the Abbasid caliphs, and it arrived in a culture already arguing about reason.
A school of theologians called the Mu'tazila held that reason alone could tell right from wrong, that God must be just, and that people have free will.
They also taught that the Quran was created rather than eternal.
In 833 the caliph al-Ma'mun began an inquisition, the mihna, requiring judges and scholars to accept this view.
The scholar Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused, and under the next caliph he was imprisoned and flogged.
A later caliph abandoned the policy around 850, and Ibn Hanbal's stand became a lasting symbol of resistance.
The question at its heart, how far reason should judge faith, runs through the philosophy that followed.
The first philosophers.
Al-Kindi, working in Baghdad in the 800s, is often called 'the philosopher of the Arabs'.
He argued that truth should be welcomed whatever its source, even foreign peoples, and that philosophy and revelation pointed in the same direction.
A generation or two later, al-Farabi, who probably came from Central Asia, became so respected as an interpreter of Aristotle that he was called 'the Second Teacher'.
He wrote on logic, music and especially politics.
Inspired partly by Plato's Republic, he described a 'virtuous city' led by a wise ruler who would guide citizens towards true happiness.
His work shaped how later thinkers connected philosophy, religion and the good society.
Avicenna's floating man.
Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was born around 980 near Bukhara, in today's Uzbekistan.
By his own account he mastered most sciences by eighteen.
His Canon of Medicine served as a medical textbook in Europe for centuries.
In philosophy, he distinguished what a thing is, its essence, from the fact that it exists: you can understand a unicorn without knowing whether any exist.
He argued for a necessary being, whose essence includes existence, identified with God.
His best-known thought experiment imagines a person created in mid-air, blindfolded, limbs apart, with no sensations.
Would they know they exist?
Avicenna said yes, taking this to show the self is distinct from the body.
It resembles Descartes's argument six centuries later.
Critics question whether imagining yourself without a body shows you could exist without one.
Al-Ghazali and Averroes.
Not everyone welcomed the philosophers' confidence.
In the late 1000s, Abu Hamid al-Ghazali wrote The Incoherence of the Philosophers, attacking Avicenna and others.
His most striking argument concerned causation.
When cotton touches fire, it burns.
But we observe only that burning follows contact, never a necessary connection.
He concluded that God directly creates each event, usually in regular patterns, so miracles are possible.
Centuries later David Hume made a similar observation for very different reasons.
In the 1100s, in Córdoba, the judge and physician Ibn Rushd, or Averroes, replied with The Incoherence of the Incoherence.
He argued that religious law itself encouraged capable people to study nature through reason.
His commentaries on Aristotle became so influential in Latin translation that Thomas Aquinas called him simply 'the Commentator'.
A shared inheritance.
This was not only a Muslim story.
The Jewish philosopher Moses Maimonides, born in Córdoba and later working in Egypt, wrote his Guide for the Perplexed in Arabic, engaging closely with Aristotle and Islamic philosophy.
Christian scholars in Spain translated Arabic works into Latin, feeding the rise of medieval European universities.
Ibn Tufayl wrote a philosophical novel about a boy raised alone on an island who reasons his way to deep truths.
It may have been known in Europe by the time of Robinson Crusoe.
It is also a myth that Islamic philosophy ended in the 1100s.
It continued to flourish, especially in Persia, with thinkers such as Mulla Sadra in the 1600s.
These debates on reason, faith and the self belong to everyone's intellectual history.
The key idea: Greek philosophy arrived in Arabic just as Muslim theologians were arguing over how far reason can judge matters of faith.
Part three. Machiavelli: the man behind ‘The Prince’.
His name became a byword for cunning and ruthlessness.
But the real Niccolò Machiavelli was a tortured civil servant, a lover of republics and perhaps the first modern political scientist.
Servant, then prisoner.
Niccolò Machiavelli was born in Florence in 1469.
In 1498, four years after the Medici were driven out, he became a senior official of the new Florentine Republic, serving as secretary of its Second Chancery.
For fourteen years he handled diplomacy and military affairs, visiting the courts of the French king, the pope and other rulers, and watching how power was gained and lost.
He also organised a citizen militia, believing Florence should not rely on hired mercenaries.
In 1512, Spanish troops helped restore the Medici, and he lost his post.
Early in 1513 his name appeared on a list of plotters and he was arrested.
He endured the strappado, hoisting by the wrists tied behind the back, reportedly without confessing.
A general amnesty freed him weeks later.
Evenings with the ancients.
Machiavelli retired, impoverished, to his small farm outside Florence.
In a famous letter to his friend Francesco Vettori in December 1513, he described his days.
He snared birds, chatted with locals and played cards at the inn.
But in the evening he went to his study, took off his muddy clothes and put on formal robes.
Then, as he put it, he entered the ancient courts of ancient men and asked them the reasons for their actions.
From those conversations with history he composed a little work on principalities.
That work was The Prince, written hoping to win back favour and employment.
It was dedicated to a member of the Medici family, but it was not published until 1532, five years after his death in 1527.
Better feared than loved.
The Prince shocked readers because it described politics as it is, not as it ought to be.
Earlier advice books urged rulers to be generous, merciful and honest.
Machiavelli argued that a ruler who always tried to be good would be ruined among so many who are not.
It is best to be both loved and feared, he wrote, but if one must choose, it is safer to be feared.
Crucially, a ruler must avoid being hated, which usually means leaving subjects' property and families alone.
A ruler should be both a fox, to recognise traps, and a lion, to frighten wolves.
His model was Cesare Borgia, who had his harsh deputy Remirro de Orco killed and displayed in Cesena.
Machiavelli's point: cruelty well used is applied once, for security, and then stops.
Fortune and virtue.
Two words run through Machiavelli's writing: fortuna and virtù.
Fortuna is luck or circumstance, the unpredictable force that can raise or ruin anyone.
Virtù does not mean moral virtue.
It means skill, energy and boldness, the capacity to seize opportunities and adapt.
Machiavelli compared fortune to a violent river that floods the plains.
When it rages, nothing can stop it, but in calm times people can build dykes and embankments to control it.
He guessed that fortune governs about half of our actions and leaves the other half to us.
A wise ruler prepares in good times and adapts quickly when circumstances change, rather than clinging to one way of acting.
The republican Machiavelli.
The common image of Machiavelli as a cheerleader for tyranny is incomplete.

His longer book, the Discourses on Livy, praises the Roman Republic and argues that free republics, where citizens share power and laws restrain ambition, are generally more stable and successful than principalities.
Even the phrase 'the ends justify the means' does not appear in his writings, although he did argue that rulers are judged by results.
In 1559 the Catholic Church placed his works on its Index of Prohibited Books, and Machiavellian came to mean scheming.
Yet many modern scholars see him as a founder of political science, one of the first to study power by observing what actually happens.
The key idea: Machiavelli spent fourteen years as a senior official of the Florentine Republic before being dismissed and tortured when the Medici returned.
Part four. Three ways to decide what's right.
Would you sacrifice one person to save five?
Philosophy's three big approaches to right and wrong, and how they help with real decisions.
Judging by results.
Ethics, or moral philosophy, asks how we should live and act.
Most of the time our instincts work fine: don't steal, keep promises, help people in need.
But instincts can conflict, and some decisions in medicine, business, technology and our own lives are genuinely hard.
Three approaches dominate: consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics.
Consequentialism says the right action has the best consequences.
Its most famous form, utilitarianism, was developed by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill: act to produce the greatest wellbeing for the greatest number.
It is practical and impartial, since everyone counts equally, and it underpins policy like cost-benefit analysis in health funding.
Australian philosopher Peter Singer is a leading modern advocate.
The trouble with results.
Imagine a surgeon with five patients who will die without organ transplants, and a healthy visitor whose organs could save them all.
Pure consequence-counting seems to say: sacrifice the visitor.
Almost everyone recoils.
The approach has other problems.
It demands that we predict consequences, which is often impossible, and it can seem to ignore justice, rights and promises.
Defenders respond that, in practice, respecting rights usually produces the best outcomes anyway.
Still, the surgeon case shows why many people feel that results cannot be the whole story.
Duties and rules.
Deontology, from the Greek for 'duty', says some actions are right or wrong in themselves, whatever the consequences.
Lying, killing innocent people and breaking promises are wrong even if they'd produce good results.
Immanuel Kant argued we should act only on principles we could want everyone to follow, and treat people as ends in themselves, never merely as means.
That explains why sacrificing the visitor is wrong: it uses him as a tool.
Human rights reflect this thinking.
Rules have problems too.
Kant argued you shouldn't lie even to a murderer asking where your friend is hiding, which strikes most people as absurd.
Duties can also conflict.
Many modern deontologists allow that duties can sometimes be outweighed, but deciding when is the hard part.
Becoming a good person.
Virtue ethics, going back to Aristotle in ancient Greece, shifts the question from 'What should I do?'
to 'What kind of person should I be?'
It focuses on developing good character traits, or virtues, like honesty, courage, compassion, fairness and wisdom.
Aristotle argued that virtues sit between extremes: courage lies between cowardice and recklessness, and generosity between stinginess and extravagance.
Good people develop practical wisdom, the ability to judge what each situation needs, through experience and habit.
Instead of a formula, virtue ethics offers a standard to grow towards.
Three lenses on a real choice.
Philosophers still haven't settled which approach is right.
In a large 2020 survey of professional philosophers, each of the three theories was favoured by roughly a third, and none came close to a majority.
So don't pick one theory.
Use all three as lenses.
Say a colleague asks you to cover up a mistake that could hurt a client.
Consequences: who is affected, and how badly?
Duties: what have I promised, and whose rights are at stake?
Character: what would a person I admire do?
Often all three agree.
When they don't, the tension shows what is really at stake, which is where good judgement begins.
A quick test: would you be comfortable if the decision appeared on the front page?
The key idea: Consequentialism judges actions by their results, and utilitarianism aims for the greatest good for the greatest number.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What does the isiZulu saying umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu mean?
Answer. A person is a person through other persons.
Question two. What was the central idea of the Mu'tazila theologians?
Answer. Human reason can judge right and wrong.
Question three. What did Machiavelli's years as a Florentine official give him?
Answer. An inside view of how power is won and lost.
Question four. What does utilitarianism say makes an action right?
Answer. It brings the greatest wellbeing overall.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
